ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 58)
        out = ALPHABET[r] + out
    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))
    return '1' * zeros + out

title: The Bitcoin Network

nodes.label: Network and nodes
nodes.body: The first section of the chapter explains that Bitcoin runs on a peer-to-peer network of nodes that are equal, and that nodes differ in the services they offer, such as keeping the whole chain or only the latest part (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In 2026 the network has about 25,000 reachable nodes, nearly all of them running Bitcoin Core or a fork (Bitnodes, 2026). This subject covers Flat network; Node kinds.

nodes.label: Flat network
nodes.body: The first subject asks what kind of network Bitcoin is: a flat peer-to-peer network without a centre, how many nodes there are today, which program they run and which services they say they offer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The numbers come from the Bitnodes snapshot of 2026-10-15 and the answers of a test node (Bitnodes, 2026). This subject covers Peers are equal; Reachable nodes today; Software share; Service bits of network.

nodes.label: Peers are equal
nodes.body: The Bitcoin network is a peer-to-peer network: every node is a peer, there is no central server, no privileged coordinator, and a node that wants to join needs only the address of one other node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This matters because there is nothing to switch off: file sharing systems such as Napster, which kept a central index, could be shut down by closing that index, whereas a network of equals goes on as long as two peers talk (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). Think of a village well where everybody carries water for everybody, against a single water tower that one person can lock. To test the claim on a machine, a small script written for this chapter, which knows nothing of Bitcoin Core except the message format, opened a connection to a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node on a private test chain and introduced itself like any other peer. The node answered with its version message (user agent /Satoshi:31.1.0/), then wtxidrelay, sendaddrv2 and verack, all framed with the magic bytes fabfb5da of that private chain; it did not ask who the script was, because the protocol has no accounts (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Reachable nodes today
nodes.body: A reachable node is one that accepts incoming connections, and the crawler Bitnodes counts them by trying to connect to every address it learns about, so its number is a lower bound of the nodes that exist, since a node behind a home router that does not listen is invisible to it (Bitnodes, 2026). The book of 2023 says that the network has about 10,000 listening nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The snapshot fetched on 2026-10-15 lists 25,361: 12,488 onion services, 7,473 on IPv4, 4,208 on I2P, 1,191 on IPv6 and one on CJDNS, so only 8,664 can be reached on the plain internet. The number has therefore more than doubled, but almost all of the growth is on the hidden networks, which is itself a result: more people want to run a node without their address being known. It is like counting the shops in a town by walking along the streets: the shops with a door on the street are counted, those that deliver only to the back door are not, and a new kind of door (the onion address) has been opened since the book was written. This example reads bitnodes_snapshot_latest.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (25361, [('cjdns', 1), ('i2p', 4208), ('ipv4', 7473), ('ipv6', 1191), ('onion', 12488)], 8664, True)

nodes.label: Software share
nodes.body: A node is defined by the rules it follows, not by the program that follows them, and in practice the great majority of nodes run the reference implementation Bitcoin Core or a fork of it, which the book states as more than 95 percent of full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the snapshot of 2026-10-15 of the 25,361 reachable nodes 25,278 (99.67 percent) report a user agent beginning /Satoshi:, of which 4,083 are Bitcoin Knots, a fork that changes policy, and 21,195 (83.57 percent of all) plain Bitcoin Core; the most common single agent is /Satoshi:31.1.0/ with 7,442 nodes (Bitnodes, 2026). The agent is only a text the node chooses for itself, as BIP 14 says, so the census shows what nodes claim, not what they run (Taaki and Strateman, 2011). The picture is a shop street in which almost every shop is a branch of one chain, with a fifth of them repainted in the colours of a relative. The consequence for safety is double: one program gives the network a common behaviour, and one program means that a single bug could reach nearly every node, and that is the argument for a diversity of implementations. This example reads bitnodes_snapshot_latest.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (25278, 4083, 21195, 99.67, 83.57, ('/Satoshi:31.1.0/', 7442), True)

nodes.label: Service bits of network
nodes.body: Every node tells its peers in the version message which services it offers, as a set of bits: NETWORK (the full block history), WITNESS (segregated witness data), BLOOM (the old filtering of BIP 37), COMPACT_FILTERS (the block filters of BIP 157), NETWORK_LIMITED (only the last 288 blocks) and P2P_V2 (the encrypted transport) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The census of 2026-10-15 counts 22,402 nodes with NETWORK, 24,582 with WITNESS, 25,322 with NETWORK_LIMITED, 7,905 with COMPACT_FILTERS, 4,308 with BLOOM and 21,768 with P2P_V2, which is 85.8 percent of all (Bitnodes, 2026). The bits matter because a new node chooses its peers by them: a light wallet looks for nodes with COMPACT_FILTERS, a node that must download the whole history looks for NETWORK. It is like the pictograms on a motorway service station sign, petrol, food, toilets: the driver reads the sign and does not go in to ask. The book's listing of getpeerinfo shows the services value 0000000000000409 with its names (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the table of the census is a list of what the nodes of today offer in addition. nodes.label: Node kinds
nodes.body: This subject asks how nodes differ in what they keep: the archival node that has all of the history and the pruned node that has only the latest, and how they say it with service bits (Schnelli, 2017). It matters because new nodes can only download the past from the first kind. This subject covers Archival node services; Pruned node services.

nodes.label: Archival node services
nodes.body: An archival full node keeps and serves every block since the genesis block, and it says so with the service bit NETWORK, which in the book is the description of a full node that keeps a complete copy of the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node that was not pruned advertised the services value 3081, which is hexadecimal c09 and decodes to NETWORK, WITNESS, NETWORK_LIMITED and P2P_V2; the node's own getnetworkinfo says so in the field localservicesnames (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The 3081 is the sum of four bits (1 + 8 + 1024 + 2048), like a menu card on which every dish has a number and the order is the sum of the numbers. The importance is practical: a new node that needs the whole history can only get it from a peer that has the NETWORK bit, and the census counts 22,402 such nodes out of 25,361, so a few thousand nodes serve the whole past for everybody else.

nodes.label: Pruned node services
nodes.body: A pruned node deletes old block files after validating them and keeps the chain state and the most recent blocks, which saves disk space but means it can no longer serve the old history; because of this it must not set the NETWORK bit and uses NETWORK_LIMITED instead, which promises at least the last 288 blocks, about two days (Schnelli, 2017). In the run a node started with the smallest possible pruning target (getblockchaininfo reports pruned true) advertised exactly WITNESS, NETWORK_LIMITED and P2P_V2, both in its network information and in the version message it sent to a peer, whereas the archival node of the same run also had NETWORK (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a librarian who has thrown out the old newspapers but keeps the last two days on the desk: the librarian can tell today's news and cannot find last year's. The book's peer listing shows the name NETWORK_LIMITED without explaining it, so BIP 159 is the place to read what it promises (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Peers and discovery
nodes.body: The second section teaches how a node joins: it finds first peers by DNS seeds, speaks a framed message protocol that begins with a version handshake, learns more addresses from its peers and keeps different kinds of connection (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything here was run against a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node on a private test chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Handshake; Discovery; Connections.

nodes.label: Handshake
nodes.body: This subject asks how two peers who have never met start to talk: the frame of every message, the version message, the protocol number, the order of the first messages and the flag that asks for silence about transactions (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). This subject covers Message framing; Version message fields; Protocol version number; Handshake message order; Relay flag silences transactions.

nodes.label: Message framing
nodes.body: Every message of the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol on the old transport is a block of bytes with a header of 24 bytes: 4 bytes of magic that name the network, 12 bytes with the command padded with zeros, 4 bytes with the length of the payload and 4 bytes with the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of the payload as a checksum (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The magic of the main chain is f9beb4d9, which chainparams.cpp writes as the four values 0xf9, 0xbe, 0xb4 and 0xd9, and the private test chain of the run uses fabfb5da (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The smallest message is verack, which has no payload at all: 24 bytes, fabfb5da, the word verack and zeros, the length 0 and the checksum 5df6e0e2 of the empty input, reproduced here by the independent code of this chapter. The frame is like the envelope of a letter: the stamp (the magic) says which postal system the letter belongs to, the label says what kind of letter it is, and the weight is written on the outside so that the receiver knows how much to read.
nodes.definition: Every message starts with a 24-byte header of magic, command, length and checksum, so the empty verack message is the 24 bytes fabfb5da76657261636b000000000000000000005df6e0e2 with the magic of the test chain, whereas the main chain uses f9beb4d9, the four bytes that chainparams.cpp sets.

nodes.label: Version message fields
nodes.body: The first message that two peers exchange is version, in which each side states its protocol version, its services, the time, the addresses it sees, a random nonce to detect a connection to itself, its user agent, the height of its chain and whether it wants transactions to be relayed to it (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The book explains the fields of the message (nLocalServices and the others) and then prints the peer listing of getpeerinfo, in which the same facts return as services, version and subver (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The version message of the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test node in the run was 102 bytes with the version 70016, the services 3081, the user agent /Satoshi:31.1.0/, the height 2099 of its chain and the relay flag true, in eleven fields that the independent parser of this chapter read. The user agent is a free text that clients set for themselves, defined in BIP 14 (Taaki and Strateman, 2011). The message is the exchange of cards at the start of a business meeting: name, position, and what each side can do for the other.

nodes.label: Protocol version number
nodes.body: The protocol version is a single number that says which messages a peer understands, and a node sends it in the version message; a feature that needs new messages is tied to a number, so that an old peer never receives a message it cannot read (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The book shows the example 70002 in its description of the handshake and in its listing, a number of 2013 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core 31.1 defines PROTOCOL_VERSION as 70016 in protocol_version.h, the node sent 70016 in the run, and the same number is the least version for wtxid relay, WTXID_RELAY_VERSION (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The number 70016 is also the one that BIP 339 and BIP 155 build on (Daftuar, 2020). A version number is like the edition number of a manual: two people who hold different editions can still work together if both can see which pages are new.

nodes.label: Handshake message order
nodes.body: A connection begins with a fixed order of messages: the initiating side sends version, the other side answers with its own version and then with the feature messages that must come before verack, wtxidrelay (BIP 339) and sendaddrv2 (BIP 155), and finally verack, the acknowledgement that the version has been accepted (Daftuar, 2020). After verack both sides may send ordinary messages: in the run the node followed verack with sendcmpct (compact blocks), ping, getheaders (what chain does the peer have), inv (what it announces) and feefilter (the minimum fee it wants), in exactly this order (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The rule that a feature message must come before verack is the reason that BIP 155 says an old peer will simply ignore it (Van der Laan, 2019). The handshake is like the greeting at a meeting of two people who do not know each other: names, then what each can do, then the nod that says we may begin.

nodes.label: Relay flag silences transactions
nodes.body: The version message has a last field, relay, which says whether the peer wants to be told about loose transactions; a node that sets it to false asks to receive blocks only, which saves bandwidth and is the base of the block-relay-only connections of Bitcoin Core (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book mentions the flag in the description of the version message (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run three peers were connected to the same node: one normal peer, one with relay false and one that had set a minimum fee with feefilter. Two transactions were created; the node announced both to the normal peer, none to the peer with relay false and only the one with the higher fee rate to the peer with the feefilter of 5 satoshis per virtual byte (Morcos, 2016). It is like a newspaper subscription with three plans: everything, only the headlines of big events, or nothing but the weekly summary, and the sender respects the plan without being asked twice.

nodes.label: Discovery
nodes.body: This subject asks how a new node finds its first peers and how it learns more: DNS seeds, the exchange of addresses with getaddr and the addrv2 format that holds the long addresses of Tor, I2P and CJDNS (Van der Laan, 2019). This subject covers DNS seed list; Addr gossip format; Addrv2 networks (BIP 155).

nodes.label: DNS seed list
nodes.body: A node that has just been installed knows no peers, and it solves the problem with DNS seeds: names that a few trusted volunteers keep pointing at the addresses of currently reachable nodes, which the node looks up once, so that it learns some addresses without any central list of nodes (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). Bitcoin Core 31.1 lists eight seeds in chainparams.cpp for the default port 8333, and the option -dnsseed is on unless the user gave -connect or limited the connections to none (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On 2026-10-15 all eight names were resolved from the sandbox and gave 182 distinct IPv4 addresses, 20 to 29 for each seed; a raw TCP connection to port 8333 of one of them could not be opened from the sandbox, so no mainnet peer was contacted and the claim is about the seeds, not the peers behind them. A seed is like the information desk at a station: you ask once, you get a handful of names, and from then on you ask the people you meet. The developer guide describes the same procedure (Bitcoin Project, 2026).

nodes.label: Addr gossip format

Gossip of this kind works like telling a stranger the names of a quarter of your friends: enough to get them started, not enough to hand over the whole address book.

nodes.label: Addrv2 networks (BIP 155)
nodes.body: The old addr message had room for 16 bytes of address, enough for IPv4 and IPv6, and it could hold the old 80-bit Tor addresses in a disguise, but not the 32-byte keys of Tor version 3, of I2P and of CJDNS; BIP 155 therefore introduced addrv2, in which each entry has a network number and an address of the length that network needs (Van der Laan, 2019). A peer that sends sendaddrv2 before verack asks to be told addresses in this form; in the run the node answered with addrv2 entries of network 1 (IPv4, 4 bytes) and network 2 (IPv6, 16 bytes), and the node's address manager held 78 IPv4 and 25 IPv6 addresses, 103 in all (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core supports the message since release 0.21.0, together with Tor version 3 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021). It is like a form with a new box for long names: the old form cut the name off after 16 letters, the new one says how long the name is.

nodes.label: Connections
nodes.body: This subject asks which kinds of connection a node keeps and why they differ: full relay, block-relay-only, addr-fetch and the others, with the limits that Bitcoin Core sets (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Connection types.

nodes.label: Connection types
nodes.body: A node does not treat all its connections alike: Bitcoin Core keeps 8 outbound full-relay connections, 2 outbound block-relay-only connections that carry no loose transactions and no addresses, which makes it harder to map the network, short-lived feeler connections that test whether an address is alive, and addr-fetch connections that only ask for addresses and leave, up to 125 connections in all (Bitcoin Core, 2026). These numbers are written as constants in net.h and the type of each connection is reported in the field connection_type of getpeerinfo, which the book lists (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run, connections of the three types were opened and read from the peer listing: outbound-full-relay and addr-fetch relayed transactions, and block-relay-only did not and spoke the v1 transport, the old plaintext one. It is like a restaurant with different tables: the regular table gets everything, the table by the kitchen door only gets what the kitchen sends out, and a few waiters walk through the room only to see if anybody is still there.

nodes.label: Block relay
nodes.body: The third section is about how a new block gets through the network quickly, because the network must carry a block within seconds if rival blocks are to remain rare: announcement with headers, compact blocks and the private networks of the miners (Corallo, 2016). It is the part of the chapter where the book is wrong about a date and where its picture is simplest. This subject covers Race and announcement; Compact blocks; Private relay.

nodes.label: Race and announcement
nodes.body: This subject asks why the speed of block announcement matters, because a slow announcement lets a rival block be found, and how the sendheaders message saves one round trip (Daftuar, 2015). This subject covers Block finding race probability; Sendheaders announcement.

nodes.label: Block finding race probability
nodes.body: Blocks are found by chance at an average of one in ten minutes, and while a new block travels through the network, other miners are still working on the old tip; if one of them finds a block in that time, two blocks compete for the same height, and one of them will be orphaned, its work wasted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). If blocks arrive as a Poisson process with an average gap of 600 seconds, the chance that a rival block appears within d seconds is 1 minus e to the power of minus d over 600; this gives 0.33 percent for 2 seconds, 1.65 percent for 10 seconds and 6.45 percent for 40 seconds, computed in the chapter's library. That is why faster block relay is a security matter and not only a comfort: the Bitcoin Optech topic page on compact block relay presents it as a way to cut the delay (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like two runners who start a relay at almost the same moment: the longer the baton takes to be passed, the more likely that somebody else has already started on the same leg.

nodes.definition: While a block is travelling a rival block can be found: with blocks as a Poisson process of one per 600 seconds the chance is 0.33 percent for a 2-second delay, 1.65 percent for 10 seconds and 6.45 percent for 40 seconds.

nodes.label: Sendheaders announcement
nodes.body: In the original protocol a node announces a new block to its peers with an inv message that holds only the hash of the block; the peer must answer with getheaders or getdata, and only then does the header arrive, which costs a round trip. BIP 130 added the message sendheaders: a peer that sends it says that new blocks should be announced directly with a headers message, and the saved text of the BIP gives the reason that it saves one round trip and the bandwidth of the hash lists (Daftuar, 2015). In the run a peer that did not send sendheaders was told of a new block by an inv message and a peer that did was sent a headers message, as the protocol says (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a shop that, instead of a card saying that a parcel has arrived for you, phones you and reads you the label: you save the walk to the counter.

nodes.label: Compact blocks
nodes.body: This subject asks how a block can be sent without repeating what the receiver has already: short ids of 6 bytes, a prefilled coinbase, a request for what is missing, two modes of sending and the depth limit, and it corrects the year of the book (Corallo, 2016). This subject covers Short ids are six bytes; Coinbase is prefilled; Missing transactions request; High and low bandwidth modes; Compact block depth limit; The year of compact blocks.

nodes.label: Short ids are six bytes
nodes.body: A compact block, defined by BIP 152, is a block that does not repeat what the receiver most likely has already: instead of each transaction it contains a short identifier of 6 bytes, computed from the transaction's wtxid with SipHash-2-4 and a key derived from the block header and a nonce (Corallo, 2016). The constant SHORTTXIDS_LENGTH of blockencodings.h is 6 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In the run a block of 13 transactions was announced as a cmpctblock message of 332 bytes where the whole block had 3,062 bytes (10.84 percent), with 12 short ids that the independent SipHash code of this chapter reproduced one by one; the same code reproduced the reference test value a129ca6149be45e5 of the SipHash paper. The saving grows with the block: a mainnet block of 1,000 transactions is shorter by a few hundred kilobytes, but this was not measured here, since the sandbox cannot reach mainnet peers. It is like a seating plan: instead of writing every guest's full name, the host writes a short code for each, because everybody in the room already knows who is who.

nodes.body: A compact block can carry a few transactions in full, the prefilled transactions, because the sender knows that the receiver cannot have them: the first one is always the coinbase transaction, which exists only inside the block and was never in anyone's mempool (Corallo, 2016). The book says that Bitcoin Core always sends a block's first transaction this way, in its description of compact blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run the compact block listed exactly one prefilled transaction, at index 0, and its transaction id was the id of the coinbase transaction of the block. The index is sent as a difference from the one before, so index 0 is a single byte. The coinbase is like the host's own name card on the table plan: all the other guests are known by a code, but nobody except the host holds that one.

nodes.label: Missing transactions request
nodes.body: When a compact block names a transaction that the receiver does not have, the receiver asks for it with getblocktxn, giving the block hash and the indexes of the missing transactions, and the sender answers with blocktxn that holds those transactions in full; with that the block is complete and can be checked as usual (Corallo, 2016). In the run the script asked with getblocktxn for the transactions at indexes 1 and 2 of the block, as if it had not had them, and the blocktxn message that came back held exactly the two transaction ids that the block lists at those positions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A missing transaction costs one round trip more, which is why the efficiency of compact blocks depends on how similar the mempools of the sender and receiver are. It is like a recipe that says use the butter you have in the fridge: if you have none, you phone and ask for it, and cooking goes on a little later.

nodes.label: High and low bandwidth modes
nodes.body: BIP 152 has two modes. In high-bandwidth mode the sender pushes the cmpctblock to a peer at once, before even validating the whole block, which is the fastest; in low-bandwidth mode it only announces the block with a headers or inv message, and the peer asks for the compact block if it wants it (Corallo, 2016). A peer picks the mode with the message sendcmpct, and because high-bandwidth mode costs the sender bandwidth when several peers are told of the same block, Bitcoin Core allows only three peers to be in that mode, which is the test lNodesAnnouncingHeaderAndIDs.size() >= 3 in net_processing.cpp (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In the run the node showed the script in its peer listing as a high-bandwidth peer (bip152_hb_to true) and sent the compact block without being asked; in low-bandwidth mode the node announced nothing by cmpctblock, and the compact block that the script then asked for was identical to the unasked one. It is like a newsagent who delivers the paper to three loyal customers at the door and keeps it on the counter for everybody else.

nodes.label: Compact block depth limit
nodes.body: A node answers a request for a compact block only if the block is recent: older blocks are sent whole, because a long time has passed and the receiver's mempool may have changed so much that a compact block would need many more round trips than a whole one. The limit is the constant MAX_CMPCTBLOCK_DEPTH = 5 in net_processing.cpp (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In the run the script asked for a block that was 20 blocks deep as a compact block and the node answered with a normal block message. The reasoning behind the limit follows from BIP 152, where compact blocks are meant to be used at the tip of the chain, where mempools agree most (Corallo, 2016). It is like the rule that you may borrow the fresh newspaper from the counter, but last month's papers have to be fetched from the archive.

nodes.label: The year of compact blocks
nodes.body: The book dates compact block relay to a release of Bitcoin Core in 2015 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is an error of the year. BIP 152 was assigned its number on 2016-04-27 according to its header, and Bitcoin Core's own table of BIPs says that the BIP is implemented as of version 0.13.0, whose release notes list compact blocks as a pull request of Suhas Daftuar (Corallo, 2016); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Release 0.13.0 appeared in August 2016 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2016). The 2015 of the book may come from the earlier work of Matt Corallo on the relay network, which was in use in 2015 but was a different thing, a separate network of servers. Dates in a book are like the dates on an old photograph: if two sources written at the time agree, they outweigh the caption.

nodes.label: Private relay
nodes.body: This subject asks how miners got blocks around faster before and beside compact blocks: private relay networks and the forward error correction of FIBRE (Corallo, 2016). This subject covers Forward error correction demonstration; Relay network history.

nodes.label: Forward error correction demonstration
nodes.body: Forward error correction adds redundant data to a message so that the receiver can rebuild parts that were lost without asking for them again, which matters on a link where a lost packet costs a whole round trip or where the sender cannot be asked; FIBRE, Matt Corallo's relay system for miners, uses it on UDP together with compact blocks (Corallo, 2016). The simplest code of this kind is parity. A message of 24 bytes was cut into four parts of 6 bytes and a fifth part was made as the XOR of the four; when one of the four was deleted, the XOR of the other three and the fifth part gave it back and the whole message was equal to the original, in the chapter's library. Real FIBRE codes are stronger, they survive several losses, but the idea is the same. The Bitcoin Optech topic page on compact block relay describes the compact block idea on which FIBRE builds (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like sending a letter with an extra page that says the sum of all the page numbers: if one page is lost on the way, the sum tells you what is missing.

nodes.definition: A message of 24 bytes cut into four parts of 6 bytes and one parity part of 6 bytes (the XOR of the four) was restored completely after one part was lost, which is the simplest form of the forward error correction that FIBRE applies to UDP packets.

nodes.label: Relay network history
nodes.body: Before compact blocks, miners built private networks for sending blocks to each other fast. The book names the relay network of Matt Corallo, created in 2015 and replaced in 2016 by a better design (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The successor is FIBRE, the Fast Internet Bitcoin Relay Engine, which according to its own site is a UDP transport with forward error correction and compact blocks (Corallo, 2016). Neither could be run in the sandbox, because both need a real network of servers, so this leaf is a claim taken from the book and the site and not recomputed. Their point is also that they are not part of the peer-to-peer protocol that every node speaks: they are extra roads that miners build for themselves, like a private motorway beside the public road. This example reads bitcoinfibre_org.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Syncing
nodes.body: The fourth section shows how a node that was offline, or never online, gets the chain: headers first, then blocks inside a download window, with the checks that stop a peer from filling the node's memory (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Headers first.

nodes.label: Headers first
nodes.body: This subject asks how a new node catches up with the chain: headers first, in batches of 2,000, then the blocks inside a window, with a protection against floods of headers (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Headers in batches of 2,000; Header chain links; Download window; Headers presync.

nodes.label: Headers in batches of 2,000
nodes.body: A new node first downloads the headers of the whole chain and only then the blocks, which is called headers-first synchronization; the node asks with getheaders and the peer answers with at most 2,000 headers in one headers message, the constant MAX_HEADERS_RESULTS in net_processing.h (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Each header in the message takes 81 bytes, the 80 bytes of the header and a zero for the number of transactions. In the run a node whose chain was 2,101 blocks high answered a request with one message of 2,000 headers (162,003 bytes) and a second of 101, and the two together equalled the height of the chain. The book describes the same process, a getheaders request answered by the first 2,000 headers in a headers message, repeated until the node has all of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like asking for the table of contents of a book first: a few pages tell you what is in it before you decide what to carry home.

nodes.label: Header chain links
nodes.body: Every block header holds the hash of the header before it, so that the headers form a chain from the genesis block to the tip, and a node can check the whole chain of headers by itself, without any block, by hashing each header twice with SHA-256 and comparing the result with the next one's previous-hash field, also checking that the work is high enough (Nakamoto, 2008). In the run the independent code of this chapter walked the 2,101 headers received from the node, 80 bytes each, and found that each one pointed at the hash of the one before it and that the last one hashed to the tip that the node reported. The book describes the header in its chapter on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and in its chapter 10 it shows lightweight clients that synchronize the headers alone. It is like a line of people who each hold the hand of the one before: you can see that nobody was skipped without asking what they carry in their bags.

nodes.label: Download window
nodes.body: Once the headers are known, the node fetches the blocks in parallel from several peers, but not too far ahead: Bitcoin Core only requests blocks inside a window of 1,024 blocks beyond the last block that it has, and it keeps at most 16 blocks in transit from one peer, so that one slow peer cannot hold up the whole download (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The two numbers are the constants BLOCK_DOWNLOAD_WINDOW and MAX_BLOCKS_IN_TRANSIT_PER_PEER of net_processing.cpp. In the run a fresh node was connected to the test node and synchronized a chain of 2,105 blocks in about 2.5 seconds, the chain then being equal to the peer's, and the getheaders request in its log was 69 bytes. The book describes the same limit as a queue of up to 1,024 blocks and adds that a node drops a peer that is too slow to deliver the oldest block in the queue, while the per-peer limit of 16 is not in the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A window is like the number of books you are allowed to take from the library at the same time: enough to keep reading, but no more than you can carry.

nodes.label: Headers presync
nodes.body: A node that has only headers cannot yet tell whether a peer's chain is true, and an attacker could send millions of low-work headers to fill its memory; Bitcoin Core therefore uses headers presync: the headers of a new peer are first only counted and hashed down to a small commitment in a phase called PRESYNC, and are stored only once the chain has been shown to have enough work (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The phase is described in headerssync.h with the words PRESYNC means the peer has not yet demonstrated their chain has sufficient work. The field presynced_headers of getpeerinfo shows how far it is, and the field is already in the listing of the book, and was present in the peer information of the run (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The protection is like a doorman who, before he lets a stranger into the club, asks him to show proof of an invitation and only then writes his name in the guest book.

nodes.label: Light clients
nodes.body: The fifth section is about nodes that do not keep the chain: simplified payment verification with headers and Merkle paths, the Bloom filters of BIP 37 that have been switched off, and the compact block filters of BIP 157 and 158 that replaced them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the section with the most numbers that can be recomputed. This subject covers Simplified payment verification (SPV); Bloom filters; Block filters.

nodes.label: Simplified payment verification (SPV)
nodes.body: This subject asks how a client with only the headers can be sure of a payment: the small size of the headers, the Merkle path and the odds of an attacker catching up as Nakamoto calculated them (Nakamoto, 2008). This subject covers Header chain size; Merkle path proof; Odds after six confirmations.

nodes.label: Header chain size
nodes.body: A lightweight client does not download the blocks; it downloads only the block headers, 80 bytes per block, and asks other nodes for proof that a payment is in a block, an idea that Satoshi Nakamoto described as simplified payment verification in the eighth section of the paper (Nakamoto, 2008). The book says that the headers are about 10,000 times smaller than the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). With the data of 2026-10-15 the claim holds almost exactly: at height 971,499 the headers total 80 x 971,500 = 77.7 megabytes, the Blockchain.com chart gives about 775,272 megabytes for the whole chain, and the ratio is 9,975 (Blockchain Charts, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). The ratio only grows with time, because every block adds 80 bytes to the headers and more than a megabyte to the chain. A library catalogue is small next to the library, and you can carry it on your phone, though you have to trust the librarian for what the shelves hold. This example reads blockchaincom_blocks_size.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (9975, 971499, 77.7, 775272, True)
nodes.definition: At the height 971,499 of the chain the 80-byte headers total 77.7 megabytes against about 775,272 megabytes for the whole chain, 9,975 times less, so the book's remark that the headers are about 10,000 times smaller is correct to three digits.

nodes.label: Merkle path proof
nodes.body: A transaction can be shown to be in a block with a Merkle path: the transactions of a block are hashed in pairs up to a single root that sits in the header, and the proof for one transaction is the hash of each sibling on the way up, so that a client with the header can recompute the root and compare (Nakamoto, 2008). In the run a block of 5 transactions needed a path of 3 hashes, since the tree for 5 leaves is three levels high; the independent code of this chapter rebuilt the root from the transaction and the path and found it equal to the root in the header, the proof message was 215 bytes against the 4,448 bytes of the block, and the node's own verifytxoutproof returned the same transaction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The path grows with the logarithm of the number of transactions, so for a block of 4,000 transactions it is about 12 hashes. It is like proving that a letter was in a sealed mailbag by showing the seals of a few other letters, so that the person with the master seal can check the whole bag.
nodes.definition: A block of 5 transactions was proven for one of them by 3 hashes whose root equals the Merkle root of the header; the proof took 215 bytes against 4,448 for the block, and the node's verifytxoutproof returned the transaction.

nodes.label: Odds after six confirmations
nodes.body: A light client cannot check the rules itself, so it trusts the work: a payment buried under six blocks is safe unless an attacker has a large share of the hash rate, and Nakamoto's paper calculates the chance that an attacker with a share q ever catches up from z blocks behind, using a Poisson distribution for the progress the attacker makes while the honest chain finds its z blocks (Nakamoto, 2008). The computation in the chapter's library gives 0.0002428 for q = 0.1 and z = 6, the value printed in the paper, and 0.1321 for q = 0.3. The headers that a client needs to watch these six blocks are small: 80 bytes x 6 blocks an hour x 24 x 365 days is 4,204,800 bytes, about 4 megabytes a year, which the paper puts as a small fraction of what a full node stores (Nakamoto, 2008). It is like a bet on a race that the chaser has already almost lost: the further ahead the leader is, the longer the odds on the chaser.
nodes.definition: Nakamoto's calculation gives an attacker with 10 percent of the hash rate a chance of 0.0002428 to catch up from 6 blocks behind, and one with 30 percent a chance of 0.1321; a header chain for 6 blocks per hour of a year is 80 x 6 x 24 x 365 = 4,204,800 bytes.

nodes.label: Bloom filters
nodes.body: This subject asks how a light client asked a full node for its transactions with a Bloom filter, how the filter works, what the messages look like and why the service was switched off by default (Hearn and Corallo, 2012). This subject covers Toy bloom filter; Bloom filter wire format (BIP 37); Merkleblock for one match; Bloom disabled by default.

nodes.label: Toy bloom filter
nodes.body: A Bloom filter is a row of bits and a few hash functions, used to ask whether an item might be in a set: to add an item, the bits at the positions given by its hashes are set; to test an item, all its positions are looked at, and a single zero means definitely not there, while all ones mean maybe there (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The book explains the filter with a row of 16 bits and the patterns A and B (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the chapter's version with three hash functions two patterns set 6 bits, both patterns are found, and a test with 20,000 random patterns said maybe in 5.3 percent of the cases although none of them had been added. The usual formula gives 3.1 percent; the exact value for six bits set out of sixteen is (6/16) to the third power, 5.27 percent, because the formula assumes a large filter. It is a doorman with a list that has been smudged: he can say definitely not on your name, but when the smudges fit, he lets someone in by mistake.
nodes.definition: A toy filter of 16 bits and 3 hash functions with two patterns added has 6 bits set, answers yes for both patterns, and for random patterns it falsely said maybe 5.3 percent of the time (the formula gives 3.1 percent), while it can say a definite no.

io.code: r = L.toy_bloom_experiment(); (r['inserted_ok'], r['bits_set'], r['fp_measured'], r['fp_formula'], r['maybe_exists'], r['nope_exists'])

nodes.label: Bloom filter wire format (BIP 37)
nodes.body: BIP 37 let a lightweight client send a Bloom filter to its peer with the message filterload, and from then on the peer sent only the transactions that matched it, together with a merkleblock for each block (Hearn and Corallo, 2012). The message holds the filter bytes, the number of hash functions, a tweak and flags; the limits of 36,000 bytes and 50 hash functions are the constants MAX_BLOOM_FILTER_SIZE and MAX_HASH_FUNCS (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The unit test of Bitcoin Core builds a filter for three elements at a false-positive rate of 0.01 and compares it to the bytes 03614e9b050000000000000001; the independent MurmurHash3 code of this chapter produced the same bytes, which shows that the description of the hash is complete and correct. Like a postal code, the filter is a short code that many addresses share, so the post office can tell you which houses might be yours but not which one exactly.
nodes.definition: The filterload message of three elements and false-positive rate 0.01 is 03614e9b050000000000000001 in the unit test of Bitcoin Core and in the independent implementation, and a filter may be at most 36,000 bytes with at most 50 hash functions.

io.code: (L.bloom_bip37_vector(), L.has('core_src_test_bloom_tests.cpp', '03614e9b050000000000000001'), L.const('core_src_common_bloom.h', 'MAX_BLOOM_FILTER_SIZE'), L.const('core_src_common_bloom.h', 'MAX_HASH_FUNCS'))

nodes.label: Merkleblock for one match
nodes.body: When a filter is loaded, the node answers a request for a filtered block with a merkleblock message: the header and a partial Merkle tree holding only the paths to the transactions that match, followed by those transactions as ordinary tx messages (Hearn and Corallo, 2012). In the run a wallet transaction was the only one to match a filter of 7 bytes with 12 hash functions; the merkleblock was 215 bytes against 4,448 bytes for the block of 5 transactions, the partial tree led to the root in the header, and the node then sent the one transaction. The book gives the same sequence in its explanation of how lightweight clients use filters (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like asking an accountant for only the pages of the ledger that mention you, with the seal of the ledger that proves they belong to it.
nodes.definition: With a filter loaded the node sent one merkleblock of 215 bytes for the block of 5 transactions (4,448 bytes) and then the one matching transaction, and the partial Merkle tree led to the root of the header.

nodes.label: Bloom disabled by default
nodes.body: Bloom filters cost the node work and, as Gervais and others showed, give the node a view of the client's addresses with weak privacy, since a node that gets the filter can often work out which addresses belong to the wallet (Gervais et al., 2014). Bitcoin Core therefore turned the service off by default: the release notes of 0.19.0.1 say that the -peerbloomfilters option now defaults to false, and the table of BIPs says that BIP 37 is disabled by default since v0.19.0 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2019). A service bit, NODE_BLOOM of BIP 111, tells the peers if it is offered (Corallo and Todd, 2015). In the run a node with default options did not set the bit and closed the connection of a peer that sent filterload, and the help text of Bitcoin Core 31.1 shows the default 0; in the census only 4,308 of 25,361 nodes set the bit. The book explains the filters at length and presents the block filters as the safer replacement of BIP 37, but it does not say that Bitcoin Core switched the service off by default in 0.19 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A shop that stopped handing out loyalty cards because they revealed what customers buy is a fair picture. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (False, True, True, 4308, True)

nodes.label: Block filters
nodes.body: This subject asks how block filters turned the question around: the node gives a compact filter of each block and the client decides what to download, with the Golomb-coded set, the parameters of BIP 158, the size of the filters and the history of the idea (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). This subject covers Golomb worked example; Golomb-Rice round trip; Basic filter parameters (BIP 158); Filter equals the node's filter; Filter bits per element; The filter skips OP_RETURN; Filter false positive rate; Block filters over the peer-to-peer network; Filter idea post of 2016.

nodes.label: Golomb worked example
nodes.body: A Golomb-coded set stores a sorted list of numbers compactly by storing the differences between neighbours, which are small, and the book explains it with the numbers 849, 653, 476, 900 and 379 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Sorted they are 379, 476, 653, 849, 900; the differences are 379, 97, 177, 196 and 51, so after the first number the largest needs 8 bits where the largest original needs 10, and adding them back gives the list again, as the chapter's code verified. The book then explains the idea with two dice, counting how often each difference 0 to 5 occurs among the 36 throws: 6, 10, 8, 6, 4 and 2, which the code confirmed. Wikipedia describes Golomb coding as a lossless method for numbers drawn from a geometric distribution (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). It is like telling someone the way by the distance from one crossing to the next, never from the start: the numbers stay short.
nodes.definition: Sorting the five numbers of the book's example gives 379 476 653 849 900, whose differences 379 97 177 196 51 need at most 8 bits where the originals need 10, and the book's table of the differences of two dice (6, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 out of 36) is right.

io.code: g = L.gcs_book_example(); (g['sorted'], g['deltas'], g['equal'], g['max_bits_original'], g['max_bits_deltas'], L.dice_table())

nodes.label: Golomb-Rice round trip
nodes.body: Golomb-Rice coding writes each difference d in two parts, the quotient d divided by 2 to the power P in unary (that many ones and a zero) and the remainder in P plain bits; the choice of P fits the code to how big the differences usually are (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). The code of this chapter coded the sorted numbers 379, 476, 653, 849 and 900 with P = 7: the result took 44 bits in 6 bytes, whereas the same five numbers with a fixed width of 10 bits would take 50, and decoding gave the same numbers back. For such a tiny list the saving is small, but real filters hold thousands of numbers. It is like writing amounts in a shop as small change plus a tally mark for each hundred: short for small amounts, and longer only when the amount is big.
nodes.definition: Golomb-Rice coding of the five numbers with parameter 7 takes 44 bits (6 bytes), against 50 bits of a fixed length of 10 bits, and decodes back to the same numbers.

nodes.label: Basic filter parameters (BIP 158)
nodes.body: The one filter type that BIP 158 defines, the basic filter, hashes every script of a block to a number in a range of N x M with SipHash-2-4 keyed by the block hash, sorts them and stores the differences with Golomb-Rice coding at P = 19, where M = 784931 (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). The constants are the result of an analysis in the BIP: P = 19 makes the filters small, and M = 784931 sets the false-positive rate to about one in 784,931 per element. The independent implementation of this chapter reproduced all 10 test vectors that the BIP publishes for testnet blocks, both the filters and the chained filter headers, and its SipHash returned the reference value a129ca6149be45e5 of the SipHash paper (Osuntokun et al., 2018). Bitcoin Core builds the same filters in blockfilter.cpp (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The two numbers are like the mesh of a net: a fixed size chosen so that nearly all fish of the wrong kind pass through.
nodes.definition: BIP 158 sets P = 19 and M = 784931 for the basic filter, the constants of the independent implementation, which reproduced all 10 test vectors of the BIP (filters and filter headers) and the SipHash reference value a129ca6149be45e5.

io.code: (L.has('bip-0158.mediawiki', 'M = 784931', 'P = 19'), P.GCS_P, P.GCS_M, L.bip158_vectors(), P.siphash_test_vector())

nodes.label: Filter equals the node's filter
nodes.body: A block filter is the compressed set of what a block touches: the output scripts of the block and the scripts of the outputs it spends, without duplicates and without OP_RETURN scripts, and the node can serve it with the RPC getblockfilter (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). In the run a block of 9 transactions gave 104 elements and a filter of 275 bytes; the independent code of this chapter, which uses only the block, the scripts of the spent outputs and the BIP, built the same 275 bytes and the same filter header, the hash of the filter chained with the header before it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). That two programs that share no code agree is the best test that a specification is complete. The book explains the filter as something that a client downloads and checks locally, which is why a faithful copy matters (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like two cooks who follow the same recipe in separate kitchens and get the same cake.
nodes.definition: The independent implementation built the filter of a block of 9 transactions, 104 elements in 275 bytes, and got the same 275 bytes and the same filter header as the node's getblockfilter.

io.code: f = R['e7_filter']; (f['my_filter_equal'], f['my_header_equal'], f['n_elements'], f['filter_bytes'], f['tx_count'])

nodes.label: Filter bits per element
nodes.body: The book explains the filter as a lossy encoding in which each output script of at least 160 bits is reduced to just 64 bits, and the 64-bit values are sorted and coded as differences (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That description is not the size of the filter. BIP 158 does not use a 64-bit range: it hashes each script into the range N x M, so that a block with 104 elements needs numbers of about 26 bits, and Golomb-Rice coding with P = 19 then stores each difference in about 21 bits (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). The filter in the run held 104 elements in 275 bytes, which is 21.15 bits per element, a third of the 64 bits of the book. A student who sized the download of filters for a wallet with the book's 64 bits would be three times too pessimistic. It is as if the shop receipt said that each item was reduced to a barcode of 64 digits, whereas the cash register keeps only the last 21.
nodes.definition: The filter of the run took 275 x 8 / 104 = 21.15 bits per element, where the book speaks of a filter that fits down to just 64 bits per element.

io.code: f = R['e7_filter']; (f['bits_per_element'], round(f['filter_bytes'] * 8 / f['n_elements'], 2), L.has('book_ch10_network.adoc', 'down to just 64 bits'))

nodes.label: The filter skips OP_RETURN
nodes.body: The basic filter leaves out every output script that starts with OP_RETURN, because such an output carries data and can never be spent, so a wallet would never look for it; BIP 158 says that the elements are all output scripts of the block and the spent ones aside from all OP_RETURN output scripts (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). The block in the run had 2 OP_RETURN outputs, none of them was in the filter, and 144 scripts reduced to 104 elements after the OP_RETURN scripts and the repeated scripts were removed; the code in blockfilter.cpp has the matching test (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book lists what goes into the filter, and the omission is a detail that is easy to miss (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like an index at the end of a book that leaves out the footnotes that nobody will look up.
nodes.example: OP_RETURN scripts are not in the filter
nodes.definition: The block of the run had 2 OP_RETURN outputs, none of them is in the filter, and its 144 scripts gave 104 elements after the OP_RETURN scripts and the duplicates were left out.

io.code: f = R['e7_filter']; (f['op_return_outputs'], f['any_op_return_in_filter'], f['scripts_total'], f['n_elements'], L.has('bip-0158.mediawiki', 'aside from all OP_RETURN output scripts'))

nodes.label: Filter false positive rate
nodes.body: A client tests its own scripts against the filter it downloaded, and a match means that the block probably holds a payment to the client; the false-positive rate of the basic filter is about 1 in M = 784,931 per script, so the client rarely downloads a block for nothing (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017). In the run 400,000 random scripts were tested against the filter of the block and one of them matched, where 0.51 matches would be expected by 400,000 / 784,931; as it was a single run the count is a plausible draw and not a measurement of the rate, and every script of the block itself matched. Because a hit costs only a download of the block, the false positives do not harm privacy as the Bloom filters did, since the client asks for blocks and not for its addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A sieve that lets one wrong grain in a million pass is good enough for a kitchen.
nodes.definition: A filter with M = 784931 is expected to match a random script once in 784,931 trials; in 400,000 trials of the run it matched once, where 0.51 matches are expected, and every script of the block matched.

io.code: p = R['e7_filter']['random_probe']; (p['m'], p['trials'], p['hits'], round(p['trials'] / p['m'], 2), R['e7_filter']['own_scripts_all_match'])

nodes.label: Block filters over the peer-to-peer network
nodes.body: BIP 157 defines how a client gets the filters over the peer-to-peer network: getcfilters asks for the filters of a range of blocks, getcfheaders for the chain of filter headers and getcfcheckpt for a checkpoint every 1,000 blocks, and a node that offers this sets the service bit COMPACT_FILTERS (Osuntokun et al., 2017). In the run a node started with -peerblockfilters=1 advertised the bit, answered a request for 3 filters with 3 cfilter messages that equalled the filter of the block, and the cfheaders and cfcheckpt messages had 162 and 34 bytes; a node without the option disconnected the asking peer. The option -peerblockfilters is off by default, as the help text of Bitcoin Core 31.1 shows, and in the census of 2026-10-15 7,905 of 25,361 nodes set the bit (Bitnodes, 2026). Neutrino, the light client of Lightning Labs, is the best known user of the protocol (Lightning Labs, 2026). This example reads bitnodes_snapshot_latest.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True, 3, [True], {'has_compact_filters_bit': False, 'disconnected': True, 'cfilters_returned': 0}, 7905)
nodes.definition: A node started with -peerblockfilters=1 advertises COMPACT_FILTERS, answers getcfilters with 3 filters equal to the block's filter, and a node without the option disconnects the asking peer; 7,905 nodes of the census advertise the bit.

nodes.label: Filter idea post of 2016
nodes.body: The idea that the client should download a small filter and test it itself came in a message to the bitcoin-dev mailing list from the anonymous developer bfd on 2016-05-09, with the title Committed Bloom filters for improved wallet performance and SPV security (Bfd, 2016). The book tells that an anonymous developer proposed it in 2016 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It became BIP 157 and BIP 158 through the work of Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod, who replaced the Bloom filter by the Golomb-coded set (Osuntokun et al., 2017). Bitcoin Core indexed the filters in release 0.19.0 and served them to peers from 0.21.0, according to the table of BIPs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The history shows how a design is moved from one forum post to a standard in about two years, a little like a recipe passed from a neighbour on a note to a cookbook. This example reads ml_bfd_2016-05_committed_bloom.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True, True, True)
nodes.definition: The idea of a filter that the client downloads and tests locally came from an anonymous post to the bitcoin-dev list on 2016-05-09 and was written up as BIP 157 and 158 by Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod, as the book says.

nodes.label: Privacy and transport
nodes.body: The sixth section is about who can see a node's traffic and where it is: the encrypted v2 transport, which is the largest change since the book, the Tor, I2P and CJDNS networks and the attacks on the network (Mehta et al., 2019). The book says the traffic is in the clear, and that is no longer true of the default. This subject covers Encrypted transport; Anonymity networks; Network attacks.

nodes.label: Encrypted transport
nodes.body: This subject asks what an observer can see of a connection: everything on the old transport, almost nothing on the v2 transport of BIP 324, which is on by default since release 27.0 and which still does not say who the peer is (Mehta et al., 2019). This subject covers Plaintext v1 transport; Encrypted v2 transport (BIP 324); Default history of the v2 transport; Unauthenticated transport.

nodes.label: Plaintext v1 transport
nodes.body: The original transport of the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol, now called v1, sends every message as plain bytes: anybody on the path, a router, a provider or a coffee shop's Wi-Fi, can read which transactions and blocks a node sends and can tell from the first bytes that the connection is Bitcoin (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The book states that the Bitcoin network communicates entirely in the clear, even in the modern Bitcoin Core at the time of writing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run the first bytes that the script sent over a v1 connection were fabfb5da, the magic of the test chain, the word version could be read in the stream, and the session identifier that getpeerinfo reports for the connection was empty. It is like a postcard: the postman, the neighbours and the people who sort the mail can read it, and the sender cannot stop them.
nodes.example: the old transport reads like a postcard
nodes.definition: On the old v1 transport the first bytes sent were the magic fabfb5da, the word version is visible in the stream, and the session identifier of the connection is empty.

nodes.label: Encrypted v2 transport (BIP 324)
nodes.body: BIP 324 defines the v2 transport, in which the two sides first make a shared secret with a key exchange whose public keys are encoded with ElligatorSwift so that they look like random bytes, and then send every message encrypted and authenticated with the ChaCha20-Poly1305 construction, in packets of which even the length is hidden (Mehta et al., 2019). In the run a connection between two nodes used the v2 transport: the stream held neither the magic bytes nor the word version, the first 4,096 bytes had an entropy of 7.953 bits per byte (8 would be perfect noise), and both sides reported the same session identifier of 64 hexadecimal characters, which two people can compare out of band to detect an attack (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Bitcoin Optech topic page describes the aim, to make the traffic harder to recognize and to read (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The change is from the postcard to a sealed envelope that is also not marked as a Bitcoin letter.
nodes.definition: On the v2 transport of BIP 324 neither the magic nor the word version appears in the stream, the first 4,096 bytes have 7.953 bits of entropy per byte (of at most 8), and both sides hold the same 64-character session identifier.

io.code: t = R['e8_transport']['v2']; (t['contains_magic'], t['contains_version_command'], t['entropy_first_4096'], t['transport_a'], t['session_id_a'] == t['session_id_n'], len(t['session_id_a']))

nodes.label: Default history of the v2 transport
nodes.body: The v2 transport came in two steps. Bitcoin Core 26.0 added it as an option, which the release notes call off by default, and 27.0 turned it on, with the words that BIP324 v2 transport is now enabled by default (Bitcoin Core developers, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024). In the source the constant DEFAULT_V2_TRANSPORT is true, and in the census of 2026-10-15 21,768 of 25,361 nodes, 85.8 percent, advertise the service bit P2P_V2, so most of the network already speaks it (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitnodes, 2026). The book is therefore out of date on this point, because it says that Bitcoin Core communicates entirely in the clear and suggests Tor as the solution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A default matters because few people change settings: the postcard became a sealed letter for everybody when the post office changed its form, and not when each customer asked for an envelope. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True, True, 'true', 85.8, True)

nodes.label: Unauthenticated transport
nodes.body: Encryption keeps out the eavesdropper but does not say who is on the other end: BIP 324 encrypts the connection but does not authenticate the peers, so an attacker who sits on the path can still pose as the peer to both sides, a man-in-the-middle attack, or can downgrade the connection to v1, and the BIP says that it protects against passive observers only; the session identifier lets users compare and notice (Mehta et al., 2019). The earlier proposal BIP 151 also sought encryption, with an authentication option, and its status is Closed (Schnelli, 2016). The book's section on encrypted and authenticated connections presents Tor as the solution for both (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A friend who whispers to you in a crowd keeps the others from hearing, but you still have to know it is your friend.
nodes.definition: BIP 324 encrypts the connection but does not authenticate the peer, so a man in the middle remains possible and only passive eavesdropping is stopped; its predecessor BIP 151 is closed.

nodes.label: Anonymity networks
nodes.body: This subject asks how a node can hide where it is: the five networks, Tor with its automatic onion service, and the later I2P and CJDNS (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Five networks; Tor hidden service; I2P and CJDNS.

nodes.label: Five networks
nodes.body: A Bitcoin Core node can speak on five networks: IPv4 and IPv6, which is the plain internet, and onion (Tor), i2p and cjdns, three overlay networks that hide the address of a node; each has its own address format, which is why addrv2 was invented (Van der Laan, 2019). The RPC getnetworkinfo lists them with a flag reachable. In the run a normal node showed ipv4 and ipv6 as reachable and onion, i2p and cjdns as not, because they need a proxy or a local router, and a second node started with a Tor proxy at 127.0.0.1:9 showed onion as reachable (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Tor was the only overlay network in the book, which speaks of transport over Tor (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Think of five postal systems with different address forms, where a letter can only cross to another system through a gateway that the node must be told about.
nodes.definition: The node lists five networks, ipv4 and ipv6 reachable and onion, i2p and cjdns not reachable without a proxy; a node started with a proxy reported onion as reachable at 127.0.0.1:9.

nodes.label: Tor hidden service
nodes.body: Tor is an overlay network that sends traffic through three relays, each of which knows only its neighbours, and that lets a server hide itself behind an onion address that ends in .onion, so that neither side learns the other's internet address (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). A Bitcoin Core node makes an onion service by itself if a local Tor is running and the control cookie is readable: the option -listenonion defaults to 1, and doc/tor.md says how to switch it off with -listenonion=0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book describes the same behaviour from version 0.12 on and prints the log line tor: ADD_ONION successful (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Tor version 3 is the only form since release 22.0, and release 28.0 changed the local port for the incoming onion connections to 127.0.0.1:8334. The census of 2026-10-15 lists 12,488 onion nodes, half of all reachable nodes. It was not possible to start Tor in the sandbox, so no onion service was created: the claim is that of the sources and the census. Biryukov and colleagues showed in 2014 that a client's identity could be linked to its address when it was not protected this way (Biryukov et al., 2014). This example reads bitnodes_snapshot_latest.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True, True, True, True, 12488)
nodes.definition: A node creates a Tor onion service by itself when Tor's control port is there (the option -listenonion defaults to 1), 12,488 nodes of the census are onion addresses, and the book's log line tor: ADD_ONION successful is still the message.

nodes.label: I2P and CJDNS
nodes.body: I2P, the Invisible Internet Project, and CJDNS are two more overlay networks, I2P a layer of tunnels in which each application has its own destination, CJDNS an encrypted IPv6 network that routes by public keys; Bitcoin Core added I2P in release 22.0 and CJDNS in release 23.0 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2022). Each has its document in the source tree that tells how to run a node over it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The census of 2026-10-15 holds 4,208 I2P nodes, one in six of all, and one CJDNS node. The book knows only Tor, so the choice of networks in the book is shorter than in the code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An I2P node cannot be reached from the plain internet, like a house that is only on a private road: this tutorial's sandbox had neither network, so no connection was tried. This example reads bitnodes_snapshot_latest.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True, True, 4208, 1)
nodes.definition: Support for I2P came in release 22.0 and for CJDNS in 23.0, neither of which the book names, and the census holds 4,208 I2P nodes and one CJDNS node.

nodes.label: Network attacks
nodes.body: This subject asks how the network itself can be attacked: the eclipse attack on the choice of peers and the routing attack on the internet below the network (Heilman et al., 2015). This subject covers Eclipse attack; Routing attack.

nodes.label: Eclipse attack
nodes.body: An eclipse attack surrounds a victim node with the attacker's peers, so that the victim sees only what the attacker shows; it may then be fed a false chain, be kept away from the real one, or be used as a tool against others, such as in a double-spend (Heilman et al., 2015). Heilman, Kendler, Zohar and Goldberg showed at USENIX Security 2015 that an attacker with enough IP addresses could fill the address tables of a node, and the Bitcoin Core defences that followed include anchor connections, which a node remembers and reconnects to after a restart, and a choice of peers from different autonomous systems (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The two block-relay-only connections of Bitcoin Core are part of the answer, since they are not seen by transaction gossip. It could not be tried in the sandbox, as it needs many real addresses, so the leaf records that the paper and the defences exist in the saved copies. It is like a traveller whose phone calls are all answered by the same impostor: only a call to a number not chosen by the impostor breaks the spell. This example reads heilman_2015_eclipse.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True, True)
nodes.definition: The eclipse attack of Heilman and colleagues surrounds a victim with the attacker's addresses; the paper's title and the anchor-connection defence both stand in the saved copies.

nodes.label: Routing attack
nodes.body: A routing attack does not need any node: an attacker who controls part of the internet's routes, such as an internet provider or an autonomous system that announces false routes with BGP, can cut the network in two or delay blocks to some nodes (Apostolaki et al., 2017). Apostolaki, Zohar and Vanbever found that a few autonomous systems carry most of the traffic of the network and that a hijack of fewer than 100 prefixes can isolate about 50 percent of the mining power. The remedy is wider: encryption does not help against a route that is simply dropped, whereas peers from different networks, such as Tor, do. The attack was not run in the sandbox, as it needs the real internet. It is like a landslide that blocks a mountain road: no traveller is attacked, but if there is only one road, nobody gets through. This example reads apostolaki_2017_hijacking.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.13.18 and not in your browser: (True,)
nodes.definition: The routing attack of Apostolaki and colleagues needs control of network routes and not of nodes, and the paper states that it can isolate about 50 percent of the mining power.

nodes.label: Mempool and orphans
nodes.body: The seventh section is about the unconfirmed transactions of a node: how they are announced, how a peer filters them, why every mempool is local, and what happens to a child that arrives before its parent, which changed with the orphan handling of releases 29 to 31 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Mempool relay; Orphan pool.

nodes.label: Mempool relay
nodes.body: This subject asks how unconfirmed transactions travel: the announcement by wtxid, the minimum fee rate a peer asks for, the difference between a local mempool and the shared UTXO set and the defaults of the mempool (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Transaction announcement by wtxid; Feefilter honoured; The mempool is local, the UTXO set is shared; Mempool defaults.

nodes.label: Transaction announcement by wtxid
nodes.body: A node does not send a whole transaction to every peer: it announces it with an inv message that holds only the identifier, and the peer asks with getdata if it does not have it already; since BIP 339 the identifier is the wtxid, the hash that also covers the witness, announced with the type MSG_WTX (0x00000005) after both sides sent wtxidrelay (Daftuar, 2020). In the run the node announced both transactions to the normal peer with entries of type 5, the peer with the feefilter was announced one, and the transaction the script then fetched had the id of the one with the higher fee rate (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's description of the inventory exchange is in terms of the txid and the MSG_TX type (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wtxid closes a weakness: two transactions with the same txid but different witnesses could stop each other. How a transaction spreads also decides how well its origin is hidden, which Fanti and Viswanath studied for the trickle and diffusion spreading rules (Fanti and Viswanath, 2017). It is like a parcel label that includes the contents' checksum and not only the sender's name.
nodes.definition: With wtxid relay the transactions were announced with inv entries of type 5 (MSG_WTX) to the normal peer and to the feefilter peer, and the transaction the script received had the txid of the one with the high fee rate.

nodes.label: Feefilter honoured
nodes.body: BIP 133 gave every node a way to say what the lowest fee rate is that it wants to hear about: the message feefilter carries a number in satoshis per kilobyte, and the sender holds back every transaction below it, which saves bandwidth for the nodes with a small mempool (Morcos, 2016). In the run a peer sent feefilter for 5,000 satoshis per kilovirtual byte, that is 5 per virtual byte; of the two transactions with 2.0 and 20.0 satoshis per virtual byte the node announced only the one with 20.0, and the node's own feefilter to the script was 100, 0.1 satoshi per virtual byte, the new default minimum of release 30.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The handshake order of the run shows that the feefilter message follows verack. It is like a notice on the door of a shop: no deliveries under a certain size, and the courier who respects it does not bring the smaller parcels.
nodes.definition: A peer that sent feefilter for 5,000 satoshis per kilovirtual byte (5 per virtual byte) was announced only the transaction of 20.0 satoshis per virtual byte and not the one of 2.0, and the node's own feefilter to its peer was 100 satoshis per kilovirtual byte, 0.1 per virtual byte.

nodes.label: The mempool is local, the UTXO set is shared
nodes.body: The book says that the mempool and the orphan pool are a node's local view and may differ from node to node, whereas the UTXO set is the shared outcome of consensus (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run two connected nodes were set up so that the second asked not to be sent transactions; after the first had accepted 6 transactions, the second had 0 in its mempool, and after the next block both held the same UTXO set of 107 outputs with the same hash. The first node saw the second's relay flag as false, which is what the relay field of the version message says (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The mempool is therefore like a waiting room that is different in every building, while the UTXO set is like the land register, which must be the same in every office.
nodes.definition: Two connected nodes held 6 and 0 transactions in their mempools before a block (the second was started blocks-only and told the first not to send it transactions), and after the block both had the same UTXO set (107 outputs, the same hash), so the mempool is local and the UTXO set is shared.

nodes.label: Mempool defaults
nodes.body: The mempool has limits that are options of the node: Bitcoin Core 31.1 holds at most 300 MB in memory (-maxmempool), drops a transaction after 336 hours or 14 days (-mempoolexpiry), and, with the cluster mempool of release 31.0, allows 64 transactions in a cluster (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). In the run getmempoolinfo showed maxmempool 300,000,000 bytes, fullrbf true, limitclustercount 64 and loaded true, and the help text of the command line gives 336 as the default expiry (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book describes the mempool as a list of unconfirmed transactions without giving a number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The memory is a fixed table at a market stall: when the table is full, the cheapest goods are taken off first, and what has lain too long is thrown out.
nodes.definition: The mempool of Bitcoin Core 31.1 holds at most 300,000,000 bytes, expires transactions after 336 hours, takes replacements of any transaction (fullrbf true) and limits a cluster to 64 transactions.

nodes.label: Orphan pool
nodes.body: This subject asks what a node does with a transaction whose parent it does not know: it keeps it, asks for the parent, releases it when the parent comes and limits the memory it may use, with limits that changed in releases 29, 30 and 31 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). This subject covers Orphan waits for parent; Node requests missing parent; Parent releases orphan; Orphanage limits.

nodes.label: Orphan waits for parent
nodes.body: An orphan is a transaction whose input refers to a parent that the node does not know yet, which happens because transactions travel by different routes and a child can arrive before its parent; the node cannot check it, so it keeps it in a small separate pool, the orphanage, and does not relay it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run the script announced a child before its parent; the node asked for the child by its wtxid (an inv entry of type 5), the child did not enter the mempool (size 0), and getorphantxs listed one entry of 191 bytes, 110 virtual bytes, which came from one peer (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The data structure is in txorphanage.h and the download logic in txdownloadman.h (Bitcoin Core, 2026). An orphan is like a guest who turns up at a party before the friend who invited him: he waits in the hall until the friend arrives.
nodes.definition: A child whose parent was not known was asked for by wtxid (inv type 5), did not enter the mempool and was kept in the orphanage, where one entry of 191 bytes was listed.
