nodes.label: Node requests missing parent
nodes.body: When the node meets an orphan it does not wait for luck: it asks the peer that sent the child for the parent, with getdata for the transaction by its parent's identifier; the type 0x40000001 is MSG_WITNESS_TX, a transaction with its witness data, which BIP 144 defined (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016). In the run the node answered the orphan with getdata of type 0x40000001 for the parent's txid, which the script then sent. Release 29.0 improved this: the node now downloads missing parents from all peers who announced the orphan, so that a peer that holds the parent back cannot block it (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). This is the old trick of asking a guest at the party where his friend is; since 29.0 the host asks everybody who knows the guest.
nodes.definition: After the orphan the node asked the announcing peer for the parent with getdata type 0x40000001 (MSG_WITNESS_TX), and since release 29.0 it asks all the peers that announced the orphan.

nodes.label: Parent releases orphan
nodes.body: When the parent arrives and is accepted into the mempool, the node looks in the orphanage for transactions that spend its outputs and tries them again; each child that is now valid joins the mempool and the search repeats for the children's children until no more are found, the cascade that the book describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the run the parent was accepted, the child followed at once, both were in the mempool and the orphanage was empty again (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The cascade is the reason a chain of dependent transactions can arrive in any order and still be rebuilt. It is like the pages of a letter that arrive by different mail: the letter can be read when the first page turns up, and the later pages fall into place one after another.
nodes.definition: When the parent arrived both parent and child were in the mempool and the orphanage was empty again.

nodes.label: Orphanage limits
nodes.body: The orphanage is a place where an attacker could try to fill the memory with transactions that never become valid, and so it has limits. Until release 29 the limit was the number of orphans, 100 by default with -maxorphantx; release 30.0 replaced it with two limits, the number of entries plus a tenth of their inputs at most 3,000, and the total weight 404,000 weight units for each peer, and release 31.0 removed the option (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026). The per-peer reserve is the constant DEFAULT_RESERVED_ORPHAN_WEIGHT_PER_PEER{404'000} in txorphanage.h, which means that one peer cannot evict the orphans of the others (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book has no limit to quote, only the statement that some implementations keep an orphan pool (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a cloakroom that gives each guest the same number of hooks, so one guest cannot hang up the coats of the whole street.
nodes.definition: Release 30.0 limits the orphanage by entries plus a tenth of their inputs (at most 3,000) and by a total of 404,000 weight units times the number of peers, and release 31.0 removed the option -maxorphantx that the old limit of 100 orphans used.

findings: Background

The chapter states that the Bitcoin network is a flat peer-to-peer network with about 10,000 listening nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Bitnodes snapshot of 2026-10-15 lists 25,361 reachable nodes: 12,488 onion services, 7,473 on IPv4, 4,208 on I2P, 1,191 on IPv6 and one on CJDNS, so only 8,664 are on the plain internet, and the growth lies almost wholly in the hidden networks (Bitnodes, 2026).
Background

The software share is as the book says, more than 95 percent of full nodes on Bitcoin Core code: 25,278 of 25,361 nodes (99.67 percent) report a /Satoshi: user agent, of which 4,083 are Bitcoin Knots and 21,195 (83.57 percent of all) plain Bitcoin Core, and the most common agent is /Satoshi:31.1.0/ with 7,442 nodes. The user agent is only a text that a node chooses (Bitnodes, 2026); (Taaki and Strateman, 2011); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The book's remark that the headers are about 10,000 times smaller than the chain holds almost exactly: at height 971,499 the headers are 77.7 megabytes against 775,272 megabytes, a ratio of 9,975. The simplified payment verification of the paper needs only these (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Blockchain Charts, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Nakamoto, 2008).
Comparative analysis

The numbers of block download in the book are right in kind and incomplete in detail: Bitcoin Core answers a getheaders with at most 2,000 headers (MAX_HEADERS_RESULTS), requests blocks inside a window of 1,024 (BLOCK_DOWNLOAD_WINDOW) with at most 16 in transit from one peer, and protects itself by a presync phase for low-work headers (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The orphan pool changed three times after the book: 29.0 asks all peers that announced an orphan for its missing parents, 30.0 replaced the limit of 100 orphans by 404,000 weight units for each peer and 3,000 entries, and 31.0 removed the option -maxorphantx. The book has no limit to compare (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Compact blocks have limits that the book does not state: a short id is 6 bytes, a node sends compact blocks unasked to at most 3 high-bandwidth peers, and it answers a request for a compact block only for blocks at most 5 deep (MAX_CMPCTBLOCK_DEPTH); in the run a block of 13 transactions took 332 bytes instead of 3,062 (Corallo, 2016); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The statement that the mempool is local and the UTXO set shared is confirmed by the run, in which one node held 6 transactions and its blocks-only neighbour 0 while both held the same UTXO set of 107 outputs after a block; the defaults of the mempool, 300 MB and 336 hours, are not given by the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Transactions are announced by wtxid since BIP 339 (inv type MSG_WTX, 5), the book describes the txid form, and a peer's feefilter (BIP 133) held back the cheaper of two transactions in the run, which announced 20.0 satoshis per virtual byte and not 2.0 to a peer that asked for 5 (Daftuar, 2020); (Morcos, 2016); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Pruned nodes do not set NETWORK but NETWORK_LIMITED (BIP 159), which promises the last 288 blocks, and the census shows 25,322 nodes with that bit against 22,402 with NETWORK; the book's listing shows the bit without explaining it (Schnelli, 2017); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitnodes, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The connection types are in the code and in the peer listing: 8 outbound full-relay connections, 2 block-relay-only connections, feelers, addr-fetch and manual connections, up to 125 in all (Bitcoin Core, 2026); the book's listing shows the field connection_type but does not explain it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Erratum: the listing of getpeerinfo in the book is outdated for Bitcoin Core 31: the node of the run returned the new fields inv_to_send, last_inv_sequence, session_id and transport_protocol_type, and no startingheight, which release 31.0 hides unless -deprecatedrpc=startingheight is given (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Conclusion

Attacks on the network are real but could not be run in the sandbox: eclipse attacks need many addresses and routing attacks need control of internet routes; the papers report that an adversary with enough addresses can monopolize a node's connections, and that fewer than 100 BGP prefixes can isolate about 50 percent of the mining power; anchor connections are a defence (Heilman et al., 2015); (Apostolaki et al., 2017); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Conclusion

Erlay, the reconciliation of transaction announcements of BIP 330, is a Draft and is off by default in Bitcoin Core 31.1 (-txreconciliation default 0), so the book's picture of flooding by inv messages is still the practice; it was not run for that reason (Naumenko and Wuille, 2019); (Naumenko et al., 2019); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Conclusion

Nakamoto's calculation of an attacker's chance of catching up, which the book uses to justify light clients, gives 0.0002428 for a share of 10 percent and 6 blocks, and 0.1321 for a share of 30 percent, computed in the chapter and equal to the table of the paper; the light client's privacy was shown to be weak by the Bloom filter study of Gervais and colleagues (Nakamoto, 2008); (Gervais et al., 2014).
Conclusion

Taken together, the chapter's picture of a flat network of equal nodes remains right in principle, but its numbers (nodes, protocol version), its date of compact blocks and its 64 bits are wrong or out of date, and five defaults have moved since the book: Bloom filters off, v2 transport on, new overlay networks, new orphan limits and no startingheight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum: the book dates compact block relay to a release of 2015, whereas BIP 152 was assigned on 2016-04-27 and Bitcoin Core lists it as implemented as of version 0.13.0, whose release notes name the pull request of Suhas Daftuar (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Corallo, 2016); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2016).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: BIP 37 Bloom filters are off in Bitcoin Core, the option -peerbloomfilters having been changed to false in release 0.19.0.1; a default node in the run did not set the BLOOM bit and disconnected a peer that sent filterload, and 4,308 of the 25,361 nodes of the census still set it. The book explains the filters at length without saying this (Bitcoin Core developers, 2019); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Corallo and Todd, 2015); (Bitnodes, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: the book says that Bitcoin Core communicates entirely in the clear, but the v2 encrypted transport of BIP 324 was added as an option in 26.0 and is on by default since 27.0, DEFAULT_V2_TRANSPORT being true, and 21,768 of the 25,361 nodes of the census (85.8 percent) advertise it. In the run a v2 stream carried neither the magic nor the word version (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Mehta et al., 2019); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The v2 transport encrypts but does not authenticate: BIP 324 says that it defends against passive observers and leaves the man-in-the-middle possible, and its predecessor BIP 151 of Jonas Schnelli was closed after mixed comments (Mehta et al., 2019); (Schnelli, 2016).
Contemporary developments

The book knows only Tor as an overlay network. Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added Tor version 3 and addrv2, release 22.0 removed Tor version 2 and added I2P, release 23.0 added CJDNS, and the census holds 12,488 onion nodes, 4,208 I2P nodes and one CJDNS node (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2022); (Van der Laan, 2019); (Bitnodes, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

Changed value: the book shows the protocol version 70002 in its description of the handshake, while PROTOCOL_VERSION of Bitcoin Core 31.1 is 70016 and the node sent it in the run; the same number is the first version for wtxid relay (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Daftuar, 2020).
Contemporary developments

Erratum: the book says that each output script is reduced to just 64 bits in the lossy encoding of a block filter. BIP 158 hashes into the range N x M with M = 784931 and codes the differences with P = 19, so the stored element takes about 21 bits, and the filter of the run held 104 elements in 275 bytes, 21.15 bits per element (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017).
Contemporary developments

BIP 158 and the code of Bitcoin Core leave all OP_RETURN output scripts out of the basic filter, a detail that matters to a client that looks for data outputs; in the run 2 OP_RETURN outputs were absent from the filter, and the independent code reproduced the node's filter and filter header byte for byte, and all 10 test vectors of the BIP (Osuntokun and Akselrod, 2017); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Osuntokun et al., 2018).
Contemporary developments

The history of the block filters is as the book says: an anonymous developer wrote to the bitcoin-dev list on 2016-05-09, the idea became BIP 157 and 158, Bitcoin Core indexed the filters in 0.19.0 and served them in 0.21.0, and the service bit COMPACT_FILTERS is set by 7,905 nodes of the census, because -peerblockfilters is off by default (Bfd, 2016); (Osuntokun et al., 2017); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitnodes, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

stories.title: Sending a block as a list of short codes
stories.who: Matt Corallo, a Bitcoin Core and relay-network developer, and Suhas Daftuar, who wrote the Bitcoin Core implementation
stories.where: the bitcoin/bips repository on GitHub, and Bitcoin Core 0.13.0, released in August 2016
stories.story: On 27 April 2016 the number 152 was assigned to the BIP Compact Block Relay by Matt Corallo. His idea was that a node already knows most of the transactions of a new block from its mempool, so the block can be sent as a header, a short code of 6 bytes for each transaction and the few transactions the receiver cannot have, such as the coinbase. Bitcoin Core 0.13.0 lists compact blocks as a pull request of Suhas Daftuar, and the BIP is marked Deployed. Corallo had earlier built a relay network for miners, and the book dates the compact blocks to a release of 2015, which is a year too early. In the run of this chapter a block of 13 transactions was sent as 332 bytes instead of 3,062.
stories.lesson: Do not resend what the receiver already knows

stories.title: The filter that told on the wallet
stories.who: Mike Hearn and Matt Corallo, who wrote BIP 37, and Arthur Gervais, Srdjan Capkun, Ghassan Karame and Damian Gruber of ETH Zurich, who tested it
stories.where: the bitcoin/bips repository, the ETH Zurich security group, and Bitcoin Core 0.19, which turned the service off by default in 2019
stories.story: BIP 37 was assigned to Mike Hearn and Matt Corallo on 24 October 2012: a light client would send a Bloom filter of its addresses to a full node and receive only matching transactions. In 2014 Arthur Gervais and colleagues at ETH Zurich showed, analytically and empirically, that the reliance on Bloom filters in existing clients leaks considerable information about the addresses of the user. In 2015 BIP 111 added the service bit NODE_BLOOM so that a node could say whether it offered the service. Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 changed the option peerbloomfilters to false, and in the census of 2026-10-15 only 4,308 of 25,361 nodes still set the bit. The test node of this chapter closed the connection of a peer that sent filterload.
stories.lesson: A privacy tool can leak more than it hides
stories.source: bip-0037.mediawiki (P08), gervais_2014_bloom_privacy.html (P57), bip-0111.mediawiki (P09), core_relnotes_0.19.0.1.md (P23), bitnodes_snapshot_latest.json (P73); the run's BloomDisabledByDefault leaf

stories.title: An anonymous post turned the filter around
stories.who: an anonymous developer who wrote as bfd, and Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod, who wrote BIP 157 and 158
stories.where: the bitcoin-dev mailing list, and the Lightning Labs project Neutrino
stories.story: On Monday 9 May 2016 a developer writing as bfd posted to the bitcoin-dev list the message Committed Bloom filters for improved wallet performance and SPV security. The idea was to turn the Bloom filter around: the full node makes one small filter for each block, and the light client downloads it and tests its own addresses, so that the client never reveals them. Olaoluwa Osuntokun and Alex Akselrod wrote it as BIP 157 and BIP 158, and replaced the Bloom filter by a Golomb-coded set, a form of compression named after the mathematician Solomon Golomb. Lightning Labs built the light client Neutrino on it. The independent code of this chapter reproduced all ten test vectors of BIP 158.
stories.lesson: Reverse the question and the leak disappears

stories.title: Eight connections, one liar
stories.who: Ethan Heilman and Alison Kendler of Boston University, Aviv Zohar of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Sharon Goldberg of Boston University
stories.where: the 24th USENIX Security Symposium in Washington, D.C., 12 to 14 August 2015
stories.story: At the USENIX Security Symposium in Washington, D.C., which began on 12 August 2015, Ethan Heilman, Alison Kendler, Aviv Zohar and Sharon Goldberg presented Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network. They showed that an adversary controlling enough IP addresses could monopolize all connections to and from a victim node, and then use the victim for double spending, selfish mining or adversarial forks. They measured the resources needed with Monte Carlo simulations and experiments on live nodes, and proposed countermeasures. Bitcoin Core now keeps anchor connections and two block-relay-only connections, and chooses peers from different autonomous systems. The chapter's census shows the other side of the problem: 12,488 of 25,361 reachable nodes are onion addresses.
stories.lesson: A node is only as honest as the peers it happens to meet

stories.title: From a closed proposal to the default
stories.who: Dhruv Mehta, Tim Ruffing, Jonas Schnelli and Pieter Wuille, the authors of BIP 324; Jonas Schnelli had written the earlier BIP 151
stories.where: the bitcoin/bips repository, and the releases Bitcoin Core 26.0 (December 2023) and 27.0 (April 2024)
stories.story: Jonas Schnelli proposed encrypting peer connections in BIP 151 on 23 March 2016, a proposal that drew mixed comments and was closed with a replacement named. On 8 March 2019 BIP 324, Version 2 P2P Encrypted Transport Protocol, was assigned to Dhruv Mehta, Tim Ruffing, Jonas Schnelli and Pieter Wuille, and it replaces BIP 151. Bitcoin Core 26.0 added it as an option that is off by default, and 27.0 made it the default. The BIP is explicit that the transport is encrypted but not authenticated. In the run of this chapter the v2 stream showed neither the magic bytes nor the word version, and 21,768 of the 25,361 nodes of the census advertise the P2P_V2 bit.

lecture.title: Chapter 10: The Bitcoin Network
lecture.say: This deck explains how the Bitcoin network works: who is on it, how nodes find each other, and how blocks and payments travel. Every number on a result picture was read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1 on a test chain, or computed with the chapter's own Python library.
lecture.takeaway: How nodes find each other, pass blocks and payments, and what moved since print

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has three parts that follow the order of the chapter. Five true stories and twenty-two code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
lecture.takeaway: Three parts, twenty-two examples, five true stories

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.
lecture.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

lecture.title: One chapter, three parts
lecture.say: The chapter has three parts and 56 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and true stories. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
lecture.takeaway: Three parts; every slide today lives on this map

lecture.title: Who is on the network
lecture.say: The Bitcoin network is a crowd of ordinary computers that follow the same rules. This part shows who they are, what a node says when it first meets another, and which services it offers.
lecture.takeaway: Like a village market with no manager: every stall only talks to its neighbours.

lecture.title: Network: key concepts (1 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Who is on the network. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: The handshake: version, then verack
lecture.say: Two nodes cannot trade blocks until they have greeted each other. The first message is version, naming the software, the protocol and the chain height, and verack confirms it. This greeting was recorded from Bitcoin Core 31.1 on a test chain. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A node speaks first with version; verack accepts it

lecture.title: A message is a 24-byte frame
lecture.say: Every message starts with the same 24 bytes. The magic tells which network it belongs to, the command names the message, the length says how much follows, and the checksum guards the payload. Verack has no payload at all. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Even an empty message has a frame of 24 bytes

lecture.title: Network: key concepts (2 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards cover 5 key concepts of the part Who is on the network. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Services: what a node offers
lecture.say: Services travel as bits in the greeting. A full node offers NETWORK, meaning it can serve the whole chain, while a pruned node has deleted old blocks and leaves that bit out. Both are recorded from the same run. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A pruned node drops the NETWORK flag but keeps relaying what it has

lecture.title: Who is on the network today
lecture.say: Onion addresses are the largest group of reachable nodes, ahead of IPv4 and I2P. Almost all nodes run Bitcoin Core or its variant Knots. These counts come from one saved snapshot, so treat them as a picture of one day and not as a constant.
lecture.takeaway: A census is a snapshot of one day, not a constant

lecture.title: Peers, blocks and transactions
lecture.say: Here the node finds its first neighbours, keeps a limited set of links, and learns to pass blocks and payments on. We measure how little a compact block needs and where a payment waits.
lecture.takeaway: Like a postal service without a post office: letters pass from hand to hand.

lecture.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (1 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Peers, blocks and transactions. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: DNS seeds hand out addresses
lecture.say: A new node has no peers, so it asks the DNS seeds that are written into its code. Each seed answered with a different list of reachable nodes. The node then dials them on the default port, 8333, and learns more from there. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Eight seeds gave twenty to thirty IPv4 addresses each, for one default port

lecture.title: addr against addrv2
lecture.say: Nodes gossip addresses to each other. The old addr message has room for IPv4 and IPv6 only, while addrv2 gives each address a network id and a length, so longer onion and I2P addresses fit. A reply is capped at a share of the address book. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: addrv2 can carry Tor and I2P addresses; the old addr could not

lecture.title: Connection types and their limits
lecture.say: A node keeps different kinds of links. Full-relay links carry everything, while block-relay-only links carry blocks but no payments and no addresses, which makes them harder to spy on. The limits are constants in the source, read from the saved file. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Block-relay-only links carry no payments and no addresses

lecture.title: Eight connections, one liar
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2015-08-12. At the USENIX Security Symposium in Washington, D.C., which began on 12 August 2015, Ethan Heilman, Alison Kendler, Aviv Zohar and Sharon Goldberg presented Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network. The lesson is that a node is only as honest as the peers it happens to meet.
lecture.takeaway: A node is only as honest as the peers it happens to meet

lecture.title: Headers first: 80 bytes a block
lecture.say: A new node asks for headers before blocks. Each header is 80 bytes and a reply holds up to 2000, so in this run two replies carried the whole chain of 2101 headers. The node checks they link up, then downloads the blocks. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Two thousand headers per reply; the whole chain of headers is small

lecture.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (2 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 5 key concepts of the part Peers, blocks and transactions. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Relay by wtxid and the fee filter
lecture.say: A node announces a payment by its witness id, not by the plain id. A peer can also say that it wants only payments above a fee rate. In the run, the peer with a filter heard of the dearer payment only. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A fee filter keeps cheap payments away from a peer that does not want them

lecture.title: An orphan waits for its parent
lecture.say: A child payment can arrive before the payment it spends. The node cannot check it yet, so it keeps it aside and asks the sender for the parent. When the parent arrives, both enter the memory pool. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The node asks the sender for the parent instead of dropping the child

lecture.title: Every node has its own memory pool
lecture.say: A memory pool holds payments that are valid but not yet in a block, and each node has its own. In the run one node held six and the other none, yet the set of unspent outputs, which only blocks change, was identical on both. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Pools may differ between nodes, yet the unspent outputs agree

lecture.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (3 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 5 key concepts of the part Peers, blocks and transactions. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Compact blocks: 332 bytes, not 3,062
lecture.say: A peer already knows most payments of a new block from its memory pool. So the block travels as a header, a short id of 6 bytes per payment, and the few payments the peer cannot have. The saving here is about nine tenths. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The peer rebuilds the block from its own memory pool

lecture.title: Sending a block as a list of short codes
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2016-04-27. On 27 April 2016 the number 152 was assigned to the BIP Compact Block Relay by Matt Corallo. The lesson is that do not resend what the receiver already knows.
lecture.takeaway: Do not resend what the receiver already knows

lecture.title: Two ways to announce a compact block
lecture.say: A peer may announce first and wait to be asked, or push the compact block unasked. Pushing saves one round trip, which matters when blocks race. Announcing first wastes nothing on a peer that already has the block.
lecture.takeaway: Pushing saves a round trip; announcing first saves bandwidth

lecture.title: The block-finding race
lecture.say: Blocks arrive at random, on average every ten minutes, so while your block is still travelling someone else may find one. The longer the delay, the likelier the rival, which is why fast relay matters most to miners. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A block that travels for a minute has about a one in ten chance of a rival

lecture.title: Peers and blocks: key concepts (4 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 5 key concepts of the part Peers, blocks and transactions. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: A parity part rebuilds a lost part
lecture.say: Forward error correction sends a little extra so that losses can be repaired without asking again. The simplest form is one parity part: the XOR of all others. XOR the survivors with the parity and the lost part appears. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: One extra part, the XOR of the others, repairs any single loss

lecture.title: Light clients, privacy and transport
lecture.say: A phone cannot hold the chain, so it asks. This part follows the question: Merkle paths, the Bloom filter that told on wallets, block filters that turn the question around, and the new encrypted transport.
lecture.takeaway: Like a tourist with a map: ask the locals, and mind what your question gives away.

lecture.title: Light clients: key concepts (1 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Light clients, privacy and transport. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: A light client checks a Merkle path
lecture.say: A light client keeps only headers. To check a payment it asks a full node for the Merkle path from that payment to the root stored in the header. Recomputing the path and getting the same root proves the payment is in the block. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Three hashes link the payment to the root in the header

lecture.title: Double-spend odds by confirmations
lecture.say: An attacker tries to build a longer secret chain. Nakamoto computed the chance of ever catching up from z blocks behind. With ten percent of the hash rate it falls quickly; with thirty percent it stays large for longer. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: More confirmations make catching up far less likely

lecture.title: Light clients: key concepts (2 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Light clients, privacy and transport. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: A toy Bloom filter
lecture.say: A Bloom filter sets a few bits for each item added, and a test looks at the same bits. If one is clear, the item was definitely not added; if all are set, it may have been. The measured wrong-maybe rate follows the formula roughly. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: The filter says maybe or definitely not; the maybe can be wrong

lecture.title: Bloom filters are off by default
lecture.say: Bloom filters told full nodes which addresses a wallet owned, but Bitcoin Core now keeps the service off. A node run with defaults does not set the BLOOM bit and disconnects a peer that sends filterload, while with the option on the filter works. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A node answers filterload only when the operator turned the service on

lecture.title: The filter that told on the wallet
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2012-10-24. BIP 37 was assigned to Mike Hearn and Matt Corallo on 24 October 2012: a light client would send a Bloom filter of its addresses to a full node and receive only matching transactions. The lesson is that a privacy tool can leak more than it hides.
lecture.takeaway: A privacy tool can leak more than it hides

lecture.title: Light clients: key concepts (3 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Light clients, privacy and transport. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Golomb coding sends differences
lecture.say: A block filter is a sorted list of hash values. Instead of sending each value, send the first and then only the gaps between neighbours. The gaps are smaller than the numbers, so each needs fewer bits. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Sorted numbers differ by less than they are, so differences take fewer bits

lecture.title: Golomb-Rice coding is lossless
lecture.say: Golomb-Rice coding writes each gap as a quotient in unary followed by p remainder bits. It is lossless: decoding returns the identical list. Here it needs fewer bits than a fixed width, and for a real filter the saving is larger. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Decoding gives back the exact list, in fewer bits

lecture.title: A block filter rebuilt without Core
lecture.say: The chapter library rebuilds the basic filter of a block from the block and the scripts it spends, without using Bitcoin Core code. It matched Core's filter and filter header, and it also reproduced all ten test vectors of BIP 158. It is example 20 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Our own code produced the same filter, the same header and ten of ten vectors

lecture.title: An anonymous post turned the filter around
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2016-05-09. On Monday 9 May 2016 a developer writing as bfd posted to the bitcoin-dev list the message Committed Bloom filters for improved wallet performance and SPV security. The lesson is that reverse the question and the leak disappears.
lecture.takeaway: Reverse the question and the leak disappears

lecture.title: Light clients: key concepts (4 of 4)
lecture.say: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Light clients, privacy and transport. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 10.
lecture.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

lecture.title: Transport v1 shows its magic, v2 hides it
lecture.say: In the old transport the network magic and the word version are plain to see. In version 2 neither appears, and the stream has almost eight bits of entropy per byte, which is what random data looks like. It is encrypted, not authenticated. It is example 21 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Version 2 traffic looks like random bytes

lecture.title: From a closed proposal to the default
lecture.say: This is a true story, dated 2019-03-08. Jonas Schnelli proposed encrypting peer connections in BIP 151 on 23 March 2016, a proposal that drew mixed comments and was closed with a replacement named. The lesson is that defaults decide how private a network is.
lecture.takeaway: Defaults decide how private a network is

lecture.title: Networks a node can reach
lecture.say: A fresh node reaches the Internet over IPv4 and IPv6. A node configured for Tor reaches the onion network only, so its address is not exposed. The chapter library reads both configurations from the recorded run. It is example 22 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: A node set to Tor reaches only the onion network

lecture.title: The chapter in five lines
lecture.say: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was read from the recorded run or computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty-two examples.
lecture.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
